Great to see that my "autumn of verified checkers" prediction is actually happening!

Have you considered using lean-inductive-models to get cheap support for nested inductives?
Considered, but it's an extensional justification right?
If you can get claude to make it work, that would be amazing
Yes, right, if you can't easily get an extensional argument in your proof it won't help.

Hm. I wrote an exponential time universe level solver very early on and never improved it. Maybe that's why docs#CategoryTheory.Limits.CategoricalPullback.CatCommSqOver.transform_map_associator is taking 27 minutes to check... (it has 26 universe variables)
I'd be very interested to hear what people think of (my idea of) the "spec".

Very nice! Lots of questions:

  1. How much of this is AI-written? I've discovered a certain subset of people really don't trust an AI-written verification of a kernel. It would be good to be open about this, whatever the answer is.
  2. What parts specifically are holding you back from having a kernel that covers all of Lean's logic (including nested inductives) and is performant enough to be used as a real external kernel (without implemented_by, unsafe, etc)? Do you have a list of such parts for easy inspection?
  3. What is the part of the code that you consider your "spec"? Is it https://github.com/intgrah/metalean/blob/master/Metalean/FastChecker/Spec.lean? Also, is it written in such a way that others could target it for their kernels?
  4. Is your consistency proof modular in that it goes through the spec and not the implementation? (Or goes through the implementation to the spec and then the spec to consistency.) Again, this would be nice since people could target your spec and get as a corollary that their checker (up to TCB assumptions) is consistent.
  5. A soundness result I think all verified kernels should target is that if M is a first-order model of ZFC with omega universes, phi is a statement of first-order (or better yet, higher-order) arithmetic, the kernel/spec accepts phi, then M satisfies phi. Would it be easy to get such a statement from a small modification of your proof? (I'm currently exploring this for Con Leche.)
  6. I believe you state higher inaccessibles as an axiom exists_inaccessibles? I think it would be better stated as an assumption where needed. This would make it more usable for other theorems like the one in the last bullet, make it possible to use Comparator on your proof, make the assumption more explicit, and make it clear it is used for consistency but not the positive soundness proof.
(7) Do you think one could have a theorem connecting Con Leche's and your spec? Maybe something like if a theorem is accepted by Con Leche, then it is accepted by your ideal Lean spec?
(For 5 and 7, I'm not necessarily asking you to do this, but rather how close it is to being doable?)

1. Yes, I used AI for a lot of the proofs, (of course, a bunch are very boring indeed to do). However I'm confident I can explain all of the code! (To quantify, about 34M output tokens, using Claude Opus 5, and Fable 5.1)
  2. From the very start I chose not to implement nesteds, so I guess this is arbitrary. I think now that it's "finished", it would actually not be too hard to add nested inductives. For the unsafe code, the major thing stopping it from being efficient without unsafe, is pointer equality fast paths, and a bunch of caching optimisations. Another major PITA is the fact that Lean has primitive projections (.1, .2) which do NOT say which inductive structure they are talking about, let alone say which type parameters are involved.
  3. By spec I mean the object language and typing, so Metalean/{Syntax,Typing}, Env, Ctx, Expr, Defeq etc. The FastChecker/Spec is mostly about the specific type signatures of the checker functions that I wrote, which would presumably not be portable.
  4. Yep, the consistency proof only depends on the type theory, so none of the checker at all.
  5. Don't know too much about this, sorry!
  6. Yes, exists_inaccessibles is the axiom used. I wrote it as an axiom because I didn't want to have to thread it through everywhere. For me, the SetSemantics are clearly separated from everything so there shouldn't be any leakage, but I could make it a hypothesis too.
  7. Not really, because Con Leche is an extensional model, whereas the type theory I defined is intensional.

If someone proves that "the set of ndjson's accepted by con-leche is equal to the set of ndjson's accepted by Metalean is equal to ... [other kernels], then it is maybe an interesting question if they are still "other kernels".

I mean, on the one hand, yes they obviously are, they're separate implementations with different performance and so on.

On the other hand, when people talk about "multiple kernels", they really mean "multiple independent verifications". And ironically, when two kernels are known to exhibit the same accepting set, then are both more trusted but also "less independent".
11 messages were moved here from #Project announcements > Metalean: verified Lean kernel by Chris Henson.

@Alex Meiburg I don’t think the true accepted statements will be equal as these are not complete kernels. (But maybe I’m wrong since non-completeness could still give a path to proving a statement in another way. But it might be harder to prove.) if we had an ideal lean spec however, maybe we could prove equivalence of those.

But I don’t understand what you are saying about non-independence. Like ideal Lean shouldn’t prove different statements of arithmetic. It should only prove exactly the statements provable in ZFC+inaccessibles.
Oh, sorry you said “ndjsons”, not statements.

But even then I think the inductive-models approach and the Lean kernel could possibly accept the same ndjsons (with a complete implementation of each). It is just that we don’t currently know since no one has done the math yet.
yeah, sorry not "independent" in the sense of logical independence, "independent" in the sense of "an independent software development effort" or "independent validation of a proof". Overloaded term!

I do mean independence in that sense. Once there is a clear spec for Lean there are a few ways to independently implement the same thing with very different implementations underneith but the same accepted proofs. And even without a clear spec, sometimes (because math works out nicely), two different specs give the same thing. Again, the inductive-models approach is a nice example. I bet a complete implementations of the inductive-models approach to nested inductives is equivalent to a a more standard approach in that the same proofs would be accepted. (With the usual incomplete implementations I agree it is likely likely two independent implementations would not give the same results.)
But inductive-models is set-theoretic?

Jason: sorry, my message was mostly responding to the middle part of your message. I didn't really get a chance to write out a response to the first part, but now I have a moment!

I think that all checkers actually implement essentially the same partial algorithm for defeq testing. There's some differences in which order things get evaluated, but that fragment is terminating and confluent so I think basically everyone will agree on what does or doesn't get accepted -- and what the "missing" step of defeq-ness that doesn't get tried is.

(I'm only like 80% sure about this, esp. since I haven't actually looked at code for some of the other recent checkers, but it would be pretty surprising to me if someone did something different!)

At least in part this is because (1) you want your checker to accept Mathlib, which means accepting all the reductions that the official kernel does, (2) there's essentially no benefit (besides "interesting feasibility research") to trying other reductions that aren't done by the official kernel, and (3) any such extra steps will also cost you in performance, probably.

The one place I think kernels do differ is in universe normalization: recognizing if two universe expressions are equal out not. Eink0rn has a more complete algorithm than the official kernel (it does reductions+simplifications that the official kernel does not, while trying to avoid combinatorial explosion), while from the messages above I guess that Metalean has a complete universe normalization algorithm that takes exponential time.

(I don't know if anyone has worked out if Lean universe equality testing is coNP-complete or not, yet...?)
So, I think there will be some small differences because of universes, but otherwise I expect broadly similar behavior

And this difference could be easily gated behind a flag. Eink0rn has several different flags to control what it does or doesn't accept to be more sound/complete, or closer to the official kernel.

I think essentially any kernel would have an easy time turning on a "use the official kernel universe normalization algorithm" as a flag, and then equivalence would be proven for that mode.
Yes, L4L has it worked out that imax level algebra is co-NP complete

Alex Meiburg said:

I think that all checkers actually implement essentially the same partial algorithm for defeq testing.

What about closure-based algorithms like mine (sokonanoda)? There are a few edge cases where mine differs in accepted behaviour in subtle ways I think.

There's some differences in which order things get evaluated, but that fragment is terminating and confluent so I think basically everyone will agree on what does or doesn't get accepted -- and what the "missing" step of defeq-ness that doesn't get tried is.

I'm pretty sure it's nonterminating as well as nonconfluent (because of structure eta)

The following example of nontermination by @Arthur Adjedj:

def tautext {A B : Prop} (a : A) (b : B)
: A = B := propext (Iff.intro (λ _ => b) (λ _ => a))
def True' : Prop := ∀ A : Prop, A → A
def delta : True' → True' := λ z : True' => z _  id z
def omega : True' := λ _ a => cast (tautext id a) delta
def Omega : True' := delta omega
def f (h : True ∧ True) : Nat :=
  And.rec (motive := fun _ => Nat) (fun _ _ => 1) h
-- #reduce f (Omega _ ⟨.intro,.intro⟩)

And of course, eta is nonconfluent:

example : (fun x : Nat × Nat => Prod.mk x.fst x.snd) = (fun x : Nat × Nat => x) := rfl
#reduce fun x : Nat × Nat => Prod.mk x.fst x.snd
#reduce fun x : Nat × Nat => x

oops! Now I'm wondering where I got my wires crossed thinking it was terminating/confluent (and feeling embarrassed)
As far as I understand it, you can make it terminating by not allowing proof reduction
but you can't do that yet because we still rely on reduction of Acc.rec for the definition of wellfounded recursion
but we also know that this is avoidable
(with choice)
so with some lean core changes we might see a new common fragment of Lean (which is different from all the existing ones) that doesn't allow reduction of proof terms

Robin Arnez schrieb:

but you can't do that yet because we still rely on reduction of Acc.rec for the definition of wellfounded recursion

We no longer rely on it in practice (since lean4#5182) and the Kernel Renovation (lean4#14977) will pull the plug on that feature on the kernel side as well.
